title: Ectopic Pregnancy: Shoulder Pain, Syncope, or Severe Pelvic Pain Means Rupture Risk
bottomLine: Pregnancy with sudden severe abdominal/pelvic pain, shoulder pain, weakness, dizziness, fainting, or hemodynamic instability can indicate ruptured ectopic pregnancy and life-threatening internal bleeding. Escalate immediately.
recognize: Abnormal vaginal bleeding and unilateral pelvic pain may precede rupture; sudden severe pain, shoulder pain, weakness, dizziness, or syncope are emergency cues.
priorities: Assess ABCs/perfusion, obtain emergency obstetric/surgical help, and prepare for rapid intervention.
assessMonitor: Trend BP/HR, mental status, pain, vaginal bleeding, abdominal findings, and ordered pregnancy/imaging/lab data.
interventions: Maintain IV access/support and NPO status as ordered while facilitating urgent evaluation.
medicationSafety: Methotrexate is used only in selected stable ectopic pregnancies under prescriber management; an unstable patient with rupture signs is not a routine medication-management case.
teaching: Seek emergency care for sudden severe pelvic/abdominal pain, shoulder pain, weakness, dizziness, or fainting in pregnancy.
delegationScope: Emergency recognition/support are appropriate; diagnosis, methotrexate eligibility, and surgical decisions are provider-level.
examTrap: Waiting for heavy vaginal bleeding before treating shock signs as serious.
oneLinePearl: Ectopic bleeding can be internal—shock may be greater than visible blood loss.
sourceBasis: ACOG Tubal Ectopic Pregnancy Practice Bulletin reaffirmed 2025

title: Placenta Previa: Painless Bleeding Means Avoid Unnecessary Vaginal Examination
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Late-pregnancy painless vaginal bleeding raises concern for placenta previa. Protect maternal-fetal stability and avoid digital vaginal examination until placental location and the obstetric plan are established.
recognize: Bright-red painless bleeding later in pregnancy is characteristic but presentation varies.
priorities: Assess maternal hemodynamics and fetal status as ordered, quantify bleeding, and notify the obstetric team promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend BP/HR, bleeding amount, contractions, pain, fetal monitoring when ordered, and symptoms of anemia/shock.
interventions: Maintain pelvic-rest/exam precautions according to obstetric plan and prepare for escalation if bleeding increases.
medicationSafety: Do not independently initiate tocolysis, corticosteroids, or other obstetric therapy; gestational age and bleeding status drive orders.
teaching: Report any bleeding promptly and follow individualized activity/pelvic precautions.
delegationScope: Routine vitals may be delegated; bleeding interpretation and obstetric escalation require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Performing a digital vaginal examination on unexplained painless third-trimester bleeding before previa is excluded.
oneLinePearl: Painless late-pregnancy bleeding: think previa and protect against provoking more bleeding.

title: Placental Abruption: Painful Bleeding Can Be Partly Concealed
bottomLine: Placental abruption can cause painful vaginal bleeding, abdominal/back pain, uterine tenderness or hypertonicity, fetal compromise, and major maternal blood loss. Visible bleeding may underestimate severity because bleeding can be concealed.
recognize: Pain, tender/firm uterus, contractions, fetal changes, and shock out of proportion to visible bleeding increase concern.
priorities: Assess maternal ABCs/perfusion and fetal status, summon obstetric help, and prepare for hemorrhage management.
assessMonitor: Trend vital signs, pain, uterine findings, bleeding, mental status, fetal monitoring, and ordered coagulation/labs.
interventions: Maintain ordered IV access/fluids and emergency readiness; avoid delaying escalation to quantify every pad first.
medicationSafety: Blood products and obstetric medications require ordered protocols and close monitoring.
teaching: Seek urgent care for bleeding with abdominal/back pain or sudden persistent uterine pain.
delegationScope: Routine measurements may be delegated; hemorrhage/fetal compromise interpretation requires licensed escalation.
examTrap: Using the amount of external bleeding to rule out severe abruption.
oneLinePearl: Abruption can hide blood—maternal and fetal condition outrank visible volume.
sourceBasis: ACOG antenatal surveillance guidance on placental abruption

title: Preeclampsia Severe Features: Headache, Vision Change, RUQ Pain, Pulmonary Symptoms Escalate
bottomLine: Preeclampsia can worsen rapidly. Severe headache, visual symptoms, upper abdominal/RUQ pain, pulmonary edema symptoms, severe-range blood pressure, low platelets, or kidney/liver dysfunction are severe-feature cues requiring urgent obstetric evaluation.
recognize: Symptoms may precede seizure or major organ complications.
priorities: Repeat/verify abnormal BP according to protocol, assess neurologic/respiratory symptoms, and notify the obstetric team immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, headache/vision, RUQ pain, reflex/neuro status as ordered, respiratory symptoms, edema/weight trends, urine output, platelets, renal/liver labs, and fetal status.
interventions: Institute seizure/fall precautions and quiet environment as ordered; prepare for magnesium/antihypertensive therapy under protocol.
medicationSafety: Magnesium sulfate and acute antihypertensives are high-risk therapies requiring ordered monitoring; PN/LVN administration scope varies.
teaching: Report severe headache, vision change, RUQ/epigastric pain, breathing difficulty, or sudden worsening symptoms immediately.
delegationScope: Routine vitals may be delegated; severe-feature recognition and high-risk medication management require licensed oversight.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient because edema is mild despite severe headache and visual changes.
oneLinePearl: In preeclampsia, symptoms of brain, liver, lung, kidney, or platelet injury signal severity.
sourceBasis: ACOG Preeclampsia and High Blood Pressure During Pregnancy guidance

title: HELLP Syndrome: RUQ Pain and Falling Platelets Can Signal Maternal Deterioration
bottomLine: Hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets can develop with hypertensive pregnancy disease. New RUQ/epigastric pain, nausea, malaise, headache, hypertension, or abnormal labs requires urgent obstetric escalation.
recognize: Symptoms can resemble GI illness; laboratory trends and maternal context matter.
priorities: Assess maternal stability and bleeding/neuro symptoms and immediately report suspected HELLP/severe preeclampsia.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, pain, platelet count, liver enzymes, hemolysis markers as ordered, urine output, neurologic status, and fetal status.
interventions: Maintain seizure/hemorrhage readiness and prepare for ordered stabilization/delivery plan.
medicationSafety: Magnesium, antihypertensives, corticosteroids, and blood products are protocolized/prescriber-directed therapies.
teaching: Persistent RUQ/epigastric pain in hypertensive pregnancy warrants urgent evaluation.
delegationScope: Lab/vital collection may be delegated; interpretation and emergency response require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Treating RUQ pain as reflux without considering hypertensive pregnancy complications.
oneLinePearl: RUQ pain in preeclampsia is a liver warning until proven otherwise.

title: PPROM: Infection, Abruption, Cord Events, and Maternal Morbidity Drive Escalation
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Preterm prelabor rupture of membranes requires gestational-age-specific obstetric management and surveillance for infection, abruption, labor, cord complications, and fetal compromise. Fever, uterine tenderness, foul discharge, bleeding, contractions, or fetal deterioration are urgent cues.
recognize: Leakage of fluid may be subtle; repeated digital examinations can increase infection risk and should not be performed casually when membranes may be ruptured.
priorities: Notify the obstetric team, assess maternal temperature/vitals and fetal status, and follow the specific PROM evaluation plan.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, uterine tenderness, discharge, bleeding, contractions, fetal monitoring, and ordered labs.
interventions: Use infection-reduction precautions and follow gestational-age-specific orders; counseling and delivery/expectant decisions are provider-led and individualized.
medicationSafety: Antibiotics, corticosteroids, magnesium, tocolysis, or other therapy depend on gestational age and clinical scenario; do not generalize one protocol to all PPROM.
teaching: Report fever, bleeding, pain/contractions, decreased fetal movement, or foul-smelling fluid immediately.
delegationScope: Routine measurements may be delegated; PPROM evaluation/management decisions require obstetric oversight.
examTrap: Performing repeated digital vaginal exams to confirm leaking fluid.
oneLinePearl: With PPROM, watch mother and fetus for infection, bleeding, labor, and cord compromise.
sourceBasis: ACOG Prelabor Rupture of Membranes Practice Bulletin reaffirmed 2023 with 2025 Practice Advisory

title: Hyperemesis: Dehydration and Electrolyte Injury Matter More Than Morning Sickness Labels
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Persistent pregnancy vomiting with inability to maintain intake can cause dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, weight loss, and thiamine deficiency risk. Escalate oliguria, orthostasis, confusion, severe weakness, or ongoing inability to tolerate fluids.
recognize: Dry mucosa, tachycardia, dizziness, reduced urine, weight loss, ketonuria/lab abnormalities when assessed, and inability to keep fluids down suggest more than routine nausea.
priorities: Assess hydration/perfusion and intake/output and notify the obstetric team for persistent or severe symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend weight, intake/output, orthostatic symptoms, electrolytes/glucose/liver testing as ordered, and nutrition status.
interventions: Provide prescribed fluids, antiemetics, nutrition support, and gradual oral intake plan.
medicationSafety: Medication selection in pregnancy is individualized; avoid unsupported OTC/herbal treatments without clinician review.
teaching: Seek care when vomiting prevents hydration or causes dizziness, faintness, or markedly reduced urine.
delegationScope: I/O and weight may be delegated; deterioration interpretation and IV/medication care follow licensed scope.
examTrap: Calling all vomiting in pregnancy normal despite oliguria and orthostatic symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Pregnancy nausea becomes dangerous when hydration, electrolytes, or nutrition fail.

title: Decreased Fetal Movement: Do Not Reassure Without Evaluation
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A meaningful decrease from the patient's usual fetal movement pattern requires timely obstetric evaluation according to the pregnancy plan. Do not dismiss the report because fetal heart tones were normal at an earlier visit.
recognize: The patient's perception of a significant change from usual movement is itself an important cue.
priorities: Notify the obstetric team and arrange/perform ordered fetal assessment rather than offering unverified reassurance.
assessMonitor: Clarify onset, baseline pattern, gestational age, associated bleeding/fluid leakage/pain, and ordered fetal surveillance findings.
interventions: Follow the institution's fetal movement and surveillance pathway.
medicationSafety: Medication is not the first response to decreased movement; evaluate fetal status.
teaching: Know the care team's instructions for changes in fetal movement and seek evaluation for a marked decrease.
delegationScope: History collection may be shared; interpretation and fetal-surveillance decisions require obstetric clinical judgment.
examTrap: Telling the patient to wait until tomorrow because the fetus may simply be sleeping.
oneLinePearl: A major change in fetal movement deserves assessment, not reassurance by phone alone.

title: Gestational Diabetes Illness: Vomiting and Hyperglycemia Need Ketone/Deterioration Awareness
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Pregnant patients with diabetes can deteriorate during illness. Persistent vomiting, inability to eat/drink, marked hyperglycemia, ketone concerns, dehydration, or reduced fetal movement requires prompt obstetric/diabetes-plan escalation.
recognize: Pregnancy changes metabolic risk; severe illness should not be managed by simply skipping insulin because food intake is poor.
priorities: Follow individualized sick-day glucose/ketone and medication plan and contact the obstetric/diabetes team for abnormal findings.
assessMonitor: Track glucose per plan, hydration, vomiting, ketones when ordered, medication intake, and fetal movement/status.
interventions: Support prescribed fluids/nutrition/insulin plan and urgent evaluation when unable to maintain intake or metabolic status.
medicationSafety: Do not independently stop insulin or adjust doses without the established plan/authorized clinician.
teaching: Have a written pregnancy-specific sick-day plan and know when to seek urgent care.
delegationScope: Glucose measurement may be delegated if trained; interpretation and insulin adjustments require authorized oversight.
examTrap: Advising the patient to skip insulin entirely because she cannot keep food down.
oneLinePearl: Illness in diabetic pregnancy needs a sick-day plan, not medication improvisation.
sourceBasis: ACOG gestational/pregestational diabetes clinical update framework

title: Pregnancy Bleeding: Rh Status and Event Details Must Follow the Patient
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: When pregnancy bleeding, trauma, pregnancy loss, or procedures occur, communicate gestational age, bleeding/event details, maternal Rh status when known, and prior prophylaxis history so the obstetric team can determine whether Rh immune globulin or further testing is indicated.
recognize: Rh prophylaxis recommendations depend on pregnancy stage and clinical event and have updated over time.
priorities: Verify blood type/Rh information when available and notify the obstetric team of sensitizing-event details.
assessMonitor: Document event timing, bleeding, trauma/procedure details, prior Rh immune globulin, and pregnancy status.
interventions: Administer ordered Rh immune globulin according to current institutional/ACOG guidance.
medicationSafety: Do not assume every bleeding event at every gestational age uses the same prophylaxis protocol.
complications: Rh alloimmunization in future/current pregnancy when prophylaxis is indicated and missed
redFlags: Major trauma/bleeding without Rh status communicated
Unclear prophylaxis plan in Rh-negative patient
teaching: Tell clinicians about Rh-negative blood type and prior Rh immune globulin when receiving pregnancy-related care.
delegationScope: Rh immune globulin administration follows medication competency; determination of indication is provider/protocol based.
examTrap: Using one memorized RhIG rule for all bleeding and pregnancy-loss scenarios despite current guidance changes.
oneLinePearl: For pregnancy bleeding, carry the Rh status and event details forward so the correct current protocol can be applied.
sourceBasis: ACOG Clinical Practice Updates on Rh D immune globulin and alloimmunization
